title: Keyboard Navigation and Focus
summary: Every interactive element must be operable without a mouse — that's not a screen-reader-specific requirement, it's a keyboard one. Learn tab order, focus traps, skip links, and why :focus-visible exists.

slides.markdown:
Keyboard accessibility is often lumped in with screen-reader accessibility, but it's a genuinely separate requirement with its own user population: motor impairments that make precise mouse control difficult or impossible, switch devices that step through focusable elements sequentially, temporary situations (an injured hand), and plenty of sighted, fully-abled power users who simply prefer the keyboard for speed.

The test that catches almost every failure in this space is brutally simple and requires no assistive technology at all: **unplug the mouse and try to use the whole page.** Everything clickable should be reachable via Tab, in a sensible order, with a visible indication of where focus currently is, and every custom interactive widget should support the keys a user would reasonably expect.

This topic covers exactly that: tab order, focus management for dynamic UI like modals and route changes, skip links, and the distinction between `:focus` and `:focus-visible` that most teams get wrong on the first try.

slides.subTitle: 0, -1, and positive values
slides.markdown:
Every element that's natively interactive (`<a href>`, `<button>`, form controls) is focusable and in the tab order automatically, in DOM source order, with no attribute needed. `tabindex` changes that default, and its three value ranges behave completely differently:

- **`tabindex="0"`** — adds a non-natively-focusable element (a `<div>` used for a custom widget) into the natural tab order, at its position in the DOM. This is the value you almost always want when making a custom element focusable.
- **`tabindex="-1"`** — removes an element from the *Tab-key* sequence, while still allowing it to receive focus programmatically via JavaScript (`element.focus()`). Used constantly for focus management — moving focus to a modal heading or an error summary that a user shouldn't reach by tabbing but the code needs to focus directly.
- **Positive values (`tabindex="1"`, `"2"`, ...)** — force an element out of natural DOM order and into an explicit numeric sequence, checked *before* any `tabindex="0"` or naturally-focusable elements. This is almost universally considered an anti-pattern: it creates a tab order that no longer matches the visual/DOM order, and maintaining a consistent numbering across a growing page is fragile and easy to break.

A traditional multi-page site gets focus management for free: a full navigation resets focus to the top of the new document automatically. A single-page app (SPA) swaps content via JavaScript with no full navigation, so **nothing resets focus by default** — after a client-side route change, focus silently stays wherever it was on the old page, often on a now-removed or now-irrelevant element.

The practical consequence: a screen reader user who clicks a link expecting to land on a new page hears nothing announced at all, because focus never moved and no new content was ever brought to their attention. The fix requires deliberate code: after a route change, move focus explicitly — typically to the new page's `<h1>` (with `tabindex="-1"` added so it accepts programmatic focus despite not being natively focusable) — and often pair it with an `aria-live` region announcing something like "Navigated to Settings" so the change itself is announced even if the user doesn't immediately explore the new heading.

This is one of the most common accessibility regressions introduced specifically by adopting SPA routing, since it's invisible to anyone testing visually — the page clearly changed, so it's easy to assume the experience is complete.

slides.sectionTitle: A focus trap for an open modal

slides.subTitle: Showing focus rings only when useful
slides.markdown:
| | `:focus` | `:focus-visible` |
|---|---|---|
| Fires on | any focus, mouse click or keyboard | focus the browser judges came from keyboard/non-pointer interaction |
| Common complaint it caused | ugly focus ring appearing on every mouse click, which designers then hid with `outline: none` | designed specifically to fix that complaint without removing focus indication entirely |

The history matters for understanding why this exists: for years, teams styled `:focus` and then, annoyed by the ring appearing on every mouse click, wrote `outline: none` to remove it — which silently also removed the focus indicator for keyboard users, a serious accessibility regression that shipped constantly because it looked like a harmless style fix to anyone testing with a mouse.

`:focus-visible` fixes this at the platform level: browsers apply their own heuristic (roughly, "was the most recent interaction a keyboard press") to decide whether to match it, so `.btn:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid blue; }` shows the ring for keyboard users and stays invisible for mouse clicks, with no `outline: none` anywhere required or safe to add.

slides.sectionTitle: Tab order through a page with a modal open
slides.markdown:
Picture a page with a header nav, a page body with a "Delete account" button, and — after clicking that button — an open confirmation modal with a heading, a "Cancel" button, and a "Confirm" button.

Before the modal opens, Tab moves through header nav links, then the page body's buttons, in DOM order. The instant the modal opens, a correct implementation moves focus directly to the modal (typically its heading or first control) and the focus trap engages — Tab now cycles only between the modal's own heading (if focusable), Cancel, and Confirm, looping from Confirm back to Cancel/heading rather than escaping to the header nav or the rest of the page body, both of which remain visually present but are inert while the modal is open.

slides.sectionTitle: A modal that leaves focus behind
slides.markdown:
The single most common keyboard-accessibility bug in real modal implementations: the modal opens correctly, looks correct, and is fully readable — but keyboard focus was never actually moved into it. The user's Tab key keeps cycling through whatever was focusable on the page *behind* the modal, which they can no longer see or reasonably interact with, while the modal itself sits completely unreachable by keyboard.

This reliably passes a visual QA pass (the modal clearly "works" — it opens, displays correctly, closes) and just as reliably fails the very first keyboard-only test, because nothing about the visual result reveals where focus actually is. It's also the exact opposite problem from a missing focus trap: a missing trap lets focus escape a modal that focus never should have left; this bug is focus never entering the modal in the first place.

The fix is one explicit line at the point the modal opens — moving focus to the modal's heading or first interactive element — and it has to be paired with the trap from earlier in this topic and with restoring focus to the trigger element on close, or the three related bugs (never entering, escaping once inside, and landing nowhere on close) tend to get fixed one at a time across multiple bug reports instead of together.

Beyond the missing-focus-management bugs already covered, a few specific patterns reliably break keyboard navigation even when someone was clearly trying to be careful:

- **Positive `tabindex` values** used to "fix" a tab order issue locally almost always break it globally the moment the page grows — a new component inserted later either collides with an existing number or gets skipped because it wasn't manually numbered, and the entire scheme has to be manually renumbered to fix. Reordering the actual DOM (often achievable with CSS `order` or `flex`/`grid` visual reordering, leaving tab order alone) is almost always the better fix.
- **`outline: none` with no `:focus-visible` replacement** removes focus indication entirely for keyboard users, discussed on the previous slide, and remains one of the single most common CSS-driven accessibility regressions in real codebases.
- **Custom widgets with `tabindex="0"` but no corresponding `keydown` handler** — focusable but non-operable is arguably worse than neither, since it looks reachable to a keyboard user who then discovers pressing Enter or Space does nothing.

Each of these is a case of solving the visible symptom (an element isn't focusable, a focus ring looks ugly, a widget needs to be reachable) without solving the underlying interaction requirement.

The full manual test, worth running on every interactive component before it ships: physically avoid the mouse (or unplug it) and use only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, arrow keys, and Escape. Confirm four things specifically: every interactive element is reachable, the tab order matches the visual/logical order, there's a visible focus indicator at every single stop (not just some), and every custom widget responds to the keys a user would reasonably expect for that widget type (Escape closes a modal or dropdown, arrow keys move between tabs or menu items).

Automated tools can flag some of this — missing focus indicators, an obviously broken tabindex value — but cannot verify tab *order* makes logical sense, or that a focus trap actually traps, or that focus genuinely moves into a modal on open, since all of those require actually exercising the interaction rather than inspecting static markup. This is one of the clearest cases in the whole accessibility space where a five-minute manual pass catches real bugs an automated scan structurally cannot.

slides.sectionTitle: Build a modal that's fully keyboard-operable
slides.markdown:
This live-exercise prompt is testing the complete checklist this topic built up, and a strong answer names all of it before or while coding: focus moves into the modal on open (to its heading or first control), a focus trap keeps Tab/Shift+Tab cycling only within the modal while it's open, Escape closes the modal, and focus returns to whatever element triggered the modal once it closes.

Missing any single piece produces a specific, distinct bug: no move-on-open leaves focus on the page behind the modal; no trap lets Tab escape into that same background; no Escape handling forces mouse-only users to hunt for a close button; no restore-on-close leaves focus on `document.body` or a removed element, which reads as the keyboard silently "losing" the user's place. Naming these as four separate requirements — not one vague "make it accessible" step — is what distinguishes a complete answer from a partial one that happens to look finished.
